title: Organ Systems
description: Nervous system anatomy and cranial nerves, special senses, endocrine glands, the heart and cardiac cycle, blood and vessels, lymphatics, and respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive anatomy and physiology.

cards.title: Which meningeal layer is the innermost, a thin delicate membrane that adheres directly to the brain and spinal cord surface?
cards.body:
Pia mater

From superficial to deep the meninges are **dura mater**, **arachnoid mater** and **pia mater**. The pia follows every gyrus and sulcus.

Mnemonic: **PIA** is **P**ressed **I**nto the brain's surface; the tough mother (dura) is outermost.
cards.searchQuery: meninges pia mater innermost layer brain

cards.title: Which space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, contains cerebrospinal fluid and the large cerebral vessels?
cards.body:
Subarachnoid space

CSF circulates here and is returned to the blood through **arachnoid villi** that project into the dural venous sinuses. A lumbar puncture samples CSF from the lumbar subarachnoid space.

Watch out: the subdural space is only a potential space; bleeding there (subdural hematoma) usually comes from torn bridging veins.
cards.searchQuery: subarachnoid space CSF meninges

cards.title: Which structure in the brain's ventricles, made of capillaries covered by ependymal cells, produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid?
cards.body:
Choroid plexus

The choroid plexuses make about 500 mL of CSF per day, although total CSF volume is only about 150 mL, so it is replaced several times daily.

Example: blockage of the cerebral aqueduct causes **hydrocephalus**, because CSF produced in the lateral and third ventricles cannot drain.
cards.searchQuery: choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid ependymal cells

cards.title: Which cerebral lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
cards.body:
Occipital lobe

The occipital lobe lies at the back of the cerebrum. Damage to it can cause cortical blindness despite healthy eyes.

Tip: **frontal** = movement, planning and personality; **parietal** = somatic sensation; **temporal** = hearing and memory; **occipital** = vision.
cards.searchQuery: occipital lobe primary visual cortex

cards.title: Which gyrus, just behind the central sulcus in the parietal lobe, is the primary somatosensory cortex?
cards.body:
Postcentral gyrus

It receives touch, pressure, pain and proprioception from the opposite side of the body, mapped as the sensory homunculus. The **precentral gyrus** (frontal lobe) in front of the central sulcus is the primary motor cortex.

Mnemonic: the **post**central gyrus comes **post** (after) the central sulcus, and it is the one that **senses**.
cards.searchQuery: postcentral gyrus primary somatosensory cortex

cards.title: Which area of the inferior frontal gyrus (usually in the left hemisphere) is essential for producing speech?
cards.body:
Broca's area

Damage causes expressive (nonfluent) aphasia: speech is halting and effortful, but comprehension is relatively preserved.

Watch out: do not confuse with **Wernicke's area**, whose damage causes fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
cards.searchQuery: Broca's area expressive aphasia inferior frontal gyrus

cards.title: Which area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus is needed to understand spoken and written language?
cards.body:
Wernicke's area

Damage causes receptive (fluent) aphasia: patients speak fluently but their words make little sense, and they do not understand speech well.

Key idea: the **arcuate fasciculus** connects Wernicke's area (comprehension) to Broca's area (production).
cards.searchQuery: Wernicke's area receptive aphasia comprehension temporal lobe

cards.title: Which large band of white matter connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres?
cards.body:
Corpus callosum

It is the largest commissural tract. Cutting it (callosotomy), once used to treat severe epilepsy, produces a "split-brain" condition.

Watch out: projection fibers link the cortex with lower centers, and association fibers link regions within one hemisphere.
cards.searchQuery: corpus callosum connects cerebral hemispheres

cards.title: Which diencephalon structure acts as the main relay station sending sensory information (except smell) to the cerebral cortex?
cards.body:
Thalamus

Nearly all sensory pathways synapse in the thalamus before reaching the cortex. Olfaction is the exception, because olfactory pathways reach the cortex directly.

Watch out: the hypothalamus is just beneath the thalamus and controls homeostasis, not relay of sensory information.
cards.searchQuery: thalamus relay station sensory cortex diencephalon

cards.title: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in which midbrain structure?
cards.body:
Substantia nigra

The dark (melanin-containing) neurons project to the striatum of the **basal ganglia**. Their loss produces resting tremor, rigidity and slowed movement (bradykinesia).

Example: levodopa, a dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier, relieves symptoms.
cards.searchQuery: substantia nigra Parkinson's disease dopamine midbrain

cards.title: Which part of the spinal cord's gray matter contains the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons?
cards.body:
Ventral (anterior) horn

Motor axons leave through the **ventral root**. The dorsal horn contains interneurons that receive sensory input, and the lateral horn (T1 to L2) holds sympathetic preganglionic neurons.

Mnemonic: **V**entral = **V**oluntary movement output; sensory fibers enter via the dorsal root.
cards.searchQuery: spinal cord ventral horn somatic motor neurons

cards.title: At which vertebral level does the adult spinal cord end (the conus medullaris)? Give the level.
cards.body:
L1 to L2

Below the conus medullaris lies the **cauda equina**, a bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots. A lumbar puncture is performed below L2, usually between L3 and L4 or L4 and L5, so the cord is not harmed.

Watch out: the spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral column, so spinal segments do not match vertebral levels below the cervical region.
cards.searchQuery: spinal cord ends L1 L2 conus medullaris cauda equina

cards.title: The phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm, arises from which spinal cord segments?
cards.body:
C3 to C5

The phrenic nerve arises from the cervical plexus. Injury to the spinal cord above C3 stops breathing.

Mnemonic: "**C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive**."
Watch out: the intercostal nerves from the thoracic spinal cord supply the intercostal muscles, not the diaphragm.
cards.searchQuery: phrenic nerve C3 C4 C5 diaphragm

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN I) carries the sense of smell, passing through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone?
cards.body:
Olfactory nerve (CN I)

Olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal epithelium send axons through the cribriform plate to the **olfactory bulb**. It is purely sensory and the only sensory pathway to reach the cortex without a thalamic relay.

Example: a cribriform plate fracture can cause anosmia.
cards.searchQuery: olfactory nerve CN I smell cribriform plate

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN II) carries visual information from the retina to the brain?
cards.body:
Optic nerve (CN II)

Its axons are the axons of retinal ganglion cells and they leave the eye at the optic disc, enter the optic canal and meet at the **optic chiasm**, where nasal-retina fibers cross.

Watch out: unlike peripheral nerves, the optic nerve is a CNS tract, covered by meninges and myelinated by oligodendrocytes.
cards.searchQuery: optic nerve CN II retina optic chiasm

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN III) innervates most extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae, and carries parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil?
cards.body:
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)

It supplies the superior, inferior and medial rectus muscles and the inferior oblique. Complete palsy leaves the eye "down and out", with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

Mnemonic: **LR6 SO4** and the rest are 3: lateral rectus (CN VI), superior oblique (CN IV), the rest CN III.
cards.searchQuery: oculomotor nerve CN III extraocular muscles pupil

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique muscle of the eye?
cards.body:
Trochlear nerve (CN IV)

The superior oblique's tendon passes through a pulley (trochlea). It is the only cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and the thinnest cranial nerve.

Mnemonic: **SO4**: superior oblique is CN IV.
cards.searchQuery: trochlear nerve CN IV superior oblique

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN V) is the main sensory nerve of the face and also supplies the muscles of mastication?
cards.body:
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)

Its three sensory divisions are **V1** ophthalmic, **V2** maxillary and **V3** mandibular. Only V3 carries motor fibers, to the muscles of mastication.

Example: trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe facial pain, often triggered by touch.
cards.searchQuery: trigeminal nerve CN V face sensation mastication

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye?
cards.body:
Abducens nerve (CN VI)

The name says it all: it moves the eye away from the midline (abduction). Damage leaves the eye turned inward (medially) and causes double vision when looking laterally.

Mnemonic: **LR6**: lateral rectus is CN VI.
cards.searchQuery: abducens nerve CN VI lateral rectus

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN VII) controls the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
cards.body:
Facial nerve (CN VII)

It also supplies parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. Damage causes **Bell's palsy**, with drooping of one side of the face.

Watch out: the parotid gland is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), although the facial nerve passes through the gland.
cards.searchQuery: facial nerve CN VII facial expression taste Bell's palsy

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN VIII) carries both hearing and equilibrium information from the inner ear?
cards.body:
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)

The **cochlear** division carries hearing and the **vestibular** division carries balance. It is purely sensory.

Example: a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) causes hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance.
cards.searchQuery: vestibulocochlear nerve CN VIII hearing balance

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN IX) carries taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland?
cards.body:
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

It also carries sensation from the pharynx (the afferent limb of the gag reflex) and input from the carotid sinus baroreceptors and carotid body chemoreceptors.

Watch out: the facial nerve (CN VII) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
cards.searchQuery: glossopharyngeal nerve CN IX taste posterior tongue parotid

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN X) provides the main parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs and most of the gastrointestinal tract?
cards.body:
Vagus nerve (CN X)

It is the longest cranial nerve and slows the heart rate. It also innervates the muscles of the pharynx and larynx.

Example: vagal stimulation raises stomach acid secretion and gut motility, and slows the heart.
cards.searchQuery: vagus nerve CN X parasympathetic heart lungs gut

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN XI) innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles?
cards.body:
Accessory nerve (CN XI)

Its spinal root arises from the upper cervical spinal cord and enters the skull through the foramen magnum before leaving by the jugular foramen.

Example: injury causes weakness in shrugging the shoulder and turning the head against resistance.
cards.searchQuery: accessory nerve CN XI sternocleidomastoid trapezius

cards.title: Which cranial nerve (CN XII) supplies the muscles of the tongue?
cards.body:
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

It exits through the hypoglossal canal. With a lesion, the protruded tongue deviates **toward the injured side**.

Mnemonic: **hypo** (under) + **glossal** (tongue); it lies under the tongue.
cards.searchQuery: hypoglossal nerve CN XII tongue muscles

cards.title: Which transparent structure at the front of the eye provides most of its focusing (refractive) power?
cards.body:
Cornea

The cornea bends light more than the lens does (about two-thirds of the eye's refraction) because of the large difference in refractive index between air and cornea. It is avascular and gets oxygen from air and aqueous humor.

Watch out: the lens fine-tunes focus (accommodation) but contributes less total power.
cards.searchQuery: cornea eye refractive power focusing

cards.title: Which muscle contracts during near vision, relaxing the suspensory ligaments so the lens becomes rounder?
cards.body:
Ciliary muscle

When the ciliary muscle contracts, the tension on the zonular (suspensory) fibers falls and the elastic lens bulges, increasing its power for close objects.

Watch out: for distant vision the ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens. With age the lens stiffens (presbyopia).
cards.searchQuery: ciliary muscle accommodation lens near vision

cards.title: Which fluid, made by the ciliary body and drained at the canal of Schlemm, fills the anterior segment of the eye?
cards.body:
Aqueous humor

It nourishes the cornea and lens and maintains intraocular pressure. Blocked drainage raises the pressure and damages the optic nerve (**glaucoma**).

Watch out: the vitreous humor fills the large posterior cavity behind the lens and is not replaced.
cards.searchQuery: aqueous humor ciliary body canal of Schlemm glaucoma

cards.title: Which retinal photoreceptors, containing rhodopsin, work in dim light but do not detect color?
cards.body:
Rods

Rods are concentrated in the periphery of the retina and are most sensitive to low light. **Cones** work in bright light, detect color and give sharp central vision.

Example: vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin and causes night blindness.
cards.searchQuery: rods photoreceptors dim light rhodopsin

cards.title: Which small pit in the center of the macula, packed with cones only, gives the sharpest vision?
cards.body:
Fovea centralis

At the fovea the overlying retinal layers are pushed aside so light reaches the cones directly. There are no rods here.

Watch out: the **optic disc** is where the optic nerve leaves the eye, and it has no photoreceptors (the blind spot).
cards.searchQuery: fovea centralis macula cones visual acuity

cards.title: Which of the three auditory ossicles sits against the oval window of the cochlea?
cards.body:
Stapes

Sound is transmitted from the tympanic membrane through the malleus, incus and stapes. The stapes footplate pushes on the oval window, creating waves in the cochlear fluid.

Example: **otosclerosis** fixes the stapes to the oval window and causes conductive hearing loss.
Mnemonic: **MIS**: malleus, incus, stapes, in order from the eardrum.
cards.searchQuery: stapes ossicle oval window middle ear

cards.title: Which structure on the basilar membrane of the cochlea contains the hair cells that convert sound into nerve signals?
cards.body:
Organ of Corti

Hair cell stereocilia contact the tectorial membrane. When the basilar membrane vibrates, the stereocilia bend and open ion channels, producing a receptor potential.

Key idea: different frequencies stimulate different regions of the basilar membrane (high pitch near the base, low pitch near the apex).
cards.searchQuery: organ of Corti hair cells basilar membrane cochlea

cards.title: Which three fluid-filled structures of the inner ear detect rotational head movements?
cards.body:
Semicircular canals

Each canal has an ampulla containing a **crista ampullaris** with hair cells embedded in a gelatinous cupula. They detect angular acceleration in three planes.

Watch out: the **utricle and saccule** detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.
cards.searchQuery: semicircular canals rotational acceleration vestibular

cards.title: Which part of the pituitary is an extension of the brain (neural tissue) that stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus?
cards.body:
Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)

Axons from hypothalamic neurons end here and release **ADH** and **oxytocin** into the blood.

Watch out: the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is glandular tissue that makes its own hormones under control of hypothalamic releasing hormones.
cards.searchQuery: posterior pituitary neurohypophysis hypothalamus storage release

cards.title: Excess growth hormone in an adult, after the growth plates have closed, causes which condition with enlarged hands, feet and jaw?
cards.body:
Acromegaly

Excess GH (usually from a pituitary adenoma) in children produces **gigantism**, since the growth plates are still open.

Key idea: GH acts partly through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), made by the liver.
cards.searchQuery: acromegaly growth hormone excess adult

cards.title: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete thyroid hormones?
cards.body:
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)

TSH is released in response to hypothalamic TRH, and its secretion falls as thyroid hormone rises (negative feedback).

Watch out: TSH is a tropic hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary, not by the thyroid.
cards.searchQuery: TSH thyroid-stimulating hormone thyrotropin anterior pituitary

cards.title: Which outer zone of the adrenal cortex secretes mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone?
cards.body:
Zona glomerulosa

From outside in, the cortex zones are the glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), fasciculata (glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol) and reticularis (androgens).

Mnemonic: **GFR** = **s**alt, **s**ugar, **s**ex, from the outside in.
cards.searchQuery: zona glomerulosa adrenal cortex mineralocorticoids

cards.title: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates milk production by the mammary glands?
cards.body:
Prolactin

Prolactin secretion is inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine and stimulated by suckling and by rising estrogen late in pregnancy.

Watch out: prolactin makes milk, but **oxytocin** causes milk ejection (let-down).
cards.searchQuery: prolactin milk production anterior pituitary

cards.title: Which hormone from the thyroid's parafollicular (C) cells lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts?
cards.body:
Calcitonin

Calcitonin opposes parathyroid hormone, but it plays only a minor role in calcium regulation in adults.

Watch out: it comes from the **C cells** between follicles, not from the follicular cells that make thyroxine.
cards.searchQuery: calcitonin parafollicular cells lowers blood calcium

cards.title: Which hormone secreted by the pineal gland rises in darkness and helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle?
cards.body:
Melatonin

The pineal gland receives light information indirectly from the retina through the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus. Melatonin secretion is highest at night.

Example: melatonin supplements are used for jet lag, since they help shift the circadian rhythm.
cards.searchQuery: melatonin pineal gland circadian rhythm sleep

cards.title: Which pancreatic islet cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits release of both insulin and glucagon?
cards.body:
Delta cells

Pancreatic islets contain **alpha cells** (glucagon), **beta cells** (insulin) and **delta cells** (somatostatin). Hypothalamic somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release.

Watch out: do not confuse somatostatin (an inhibitor) with somatotropin, which is growth hormone.
cards.searchQuery: delta cells somatostatin pancreatic islets

cards.title: Which heart chamber has the thickest myocardium because it pumps blood into the systemic circuit?
cards.body:
Left ventricle

The left ventricle's wall is about three times thicker than the right's because systemic resistance is much higher than pulmonary resistance.

Watch out: both ventricles pump the same volume per beat; the difference in wall thickness reflects pressure, not volume.
cards.searchQuery: left ventricle thickest wall myocardium

cards.title: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?
cards.body:
Tricuspid valve (right AV valve)

It has three cusps. The pulmonary semilunar valve lies between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.

Mnemonic: **LAB RAT**: **L**eft **A**trium **B**icuspid, **R**ight **A**trium **T**ricuspid.
cards.searchQuery: tricuspid valve right atrioventricular valve

cards.title: Which valve, also called the bicuspid valve, lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?
cards.body:
Mitral valve

It has two cusps (anterior and posterior). Mitral valve prolapse allows blood to leak back into the left atrium during systole.

Watch out: the aortic semilunar valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta.
cards.searchQuery: mitral valve bicuspid left atrioventricular valve

cards.title: Which fibrous cords, anchored to papillary muscles, prevent the AV valve cusps from flipping into the atria during ventricular contraction?
cards.body:
Chordae tendineae

They are often called the heart strings. The papillary muscles contract with the ventricle and keep tension on the cords.

Example: rupture of the chordae or papillary muscle (for example after a heart attack) causes sudden severe valve regurgitation.
cards.searchQuery: chordae tendineae papillary muscles AV valve prolapse

cards.title: Which structure in the interatrial septum delays the electrical impulse for about 0.1 second, so the ventricles can fill before contracting?
cards.body:
Atrioventricular (AV) node

Its slowly conducting cells provide the delay. The impulse then moves through the **bundle of His**, the right and left bundle branches and the Purkinje fibers.

Watch out: the atria and ventricles are electrically insulated by the fibrous skeleton, so the AV node is the only normal electrical connection.
cards.searchQuery: AV node delay atrioventricular node conduction

cards.title: Which specialized fibers spread the impulse rapidly through the ventricular myocardium, allowing coordinated contraction from the apex upward?
cards.body:
Purkinje fibers

They conduct faster than other cardiac cells. Contraction beginning at the apex squeezes blood toward the outflow tracts.

Key idea: conduction order is SA node, atria, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches and then Purkinje fibers.
cards.searchQuery: Purkinje fibers ventricular conduction system

cards.title: Which part of a normal ECG represents ventricular depolarization?
cards.body:
QRS complex

The **P wave** is atrial depolarization and the **T wave** is ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS complex.

Example: a wide QRS suggests slowed conduction in the ventricles, as in bundle branch block.
cards.searchQuery: ECG QRS complex ventricular depolarization

cards.title: Which law states that, within limits, the greater the volume of blood filling the ventricles, the greater the force of the next contraction?
cards.body:
Frank-Starling law of the heart

Greater end-diastolic volume (preload) stretches the myocardial fibers, producing a stronger contraction and a larger stroke volume.

Why: stretch brings sarcomeres closer to optimal overlap, and increases the sensitivity of troponin C to $\ce{Ca^2+}$.
Watch out: excessive stretch (as in heart failure) reduces output.
cards.searchQuery: Frank-Starling law preload stroke volume

cards.title: Which hormone, secreted mainly by the kidneys in response to low blood oxygen, stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow?
cards.body:
Erythropoietin (EPO)

Hypoxia triggers the kidneys to release EPO, which increases the production of erythrocytes in red bone marrow. Chronic kidney disease therefore often causes anemia.

Example: living at altitude raises EPO and the hematocrit.
cards.searchQuery: erythropoietin EPO kidney red blood cell production

cards.title: About how many days does a typical erythrocyte circulate before it is destroyed? Give the number only.
cards.body:
120

Red cells lack nuclei and organelles, so they cannot repair themselves. Old cells are removed by macrophages in the spleen, liver and bone marrow.

Key idea: iron is recycled to make new hemoglobin, and the heme is converted to bilirubin.
cards.searchQuery: red blood cell lifespan 120 days spleen

cards.title: Which yellow pigment is produced when macrophages break down the heme of old red blood cells?
cards.body:
Bilirubin

Heme is converted to biliverdin (green) and then to bilirubin (yellow-orange). The liver conjugates bilirubin and excretes it in bile.

Example: excess bilirubin from liver disease or red cell breakdown causes **jaundice**, with yellowing of the skin and sclera.
cards.searchQuery: bilirubin heme breakdown jaundice

cards.title: Which white blood cell is the most abundant (about 50 to 70 percent), has a multilobed nucleus and is first to arrive at sites of bacterial infection?
cards.body:
Neutrophil

Neutrophils phagocytose bacteria and release enzymes. A high neutrophil count often indicates bacterial infection.

Mnemonic: **Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas** lists the WBCs from most to least abundant: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.
cards.searchQuery: neutrophil most abundant white blood cell bacterial infection

cards.title: Which white blood cell, with bilobed nucleus and red-orange granules, increases in parasitic worm infections and allergic reactions?
cards.body:
Eosinophil

Eosinophils release toxic proteins that kill parasitic worms too large to be phagocytosed. They also take part in allergic reactions such as asthma.

Tip: **eosin** is a red dye, so the granules stain red-orange.
cards.searchQuery: eosinophil parasitic worms allergy granules

cards.title: Which blood type is considered the universal red cell donor, because its cells lack A, B and Rh D antigens?
cards.body:
O negative

Recipients cannot make antibodies against antigens that are absent on the donor red cells. Type **AB positive** is the universal recipient of red cells.

Watch out: for plasma donation the rule reverses, and type AB plasma is universal, since it has neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies.
cards.searchQuery: O negative universal donor blood type

cards.title: Which enzyme converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin strands during blood clotting?
cards.body:
Thrombin

Thrombin is formed from prothrombin by the prothrombinase complex. Fibrin forms a meshwork that traps red cells and stabilizes the platelet plug.

Watch out: thrombin also activates platelets and factor XIII, which cross-links the fibrin.
cards.searchQuery: thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin clotting

cards.title: Which fat-soluble vitamin is required by the liver to make clotting factors II, VII, IX and X?
cards.body:
Vitamin K

Gut bacteria produce some vitamin K. Warfarin acts by blocking the recycling of vitamin K, reducing these clotting factors.

Example: newborns receive a vitamin K injection because their gut has not yet been colonized by bacteria.
cards.searchQuery: vitamin K clotting factors liver warfarin

cards.title: Which artery is the first branch off the aortic arch, dividing into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries?
cards.body:
Brachiocephalic trunk

The aortic arch gives off, in order: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery.

Watch out: only the right side has a brachiocephalic trunk; on the left the carotid and subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.
cards.searchQuery: brachiocephalic trunk aortic arch branches

cards.title: What are the three sequential steps of hemostasis after a small vessel is injured?
cards.body:
Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation and coagulation

1. **Vascular spasm**: the injured vessel constricts, reducing blood loss.
2. **Platelet plug**: platelets adhere to exposed collagen and aggregate.
3. **Coagulation**: a fibrin mesh forms and reinforces the plug into a clot.

Tip: afterward the clot retracts and is dissolved by plasmin (fibrinolysis) once the vessel has healed.
cards.searchQuery: hemostasis three steps vascular spasm platelet plug coagulation

cards.title: Which anastomosis at the base of the brain links the internal carotid and basilar artery systems, providing collateral blood flow?
cards.body:
Circle of Willis (cerebral arterial circle)

If one feeding artery is blocked, other vessels in the circle can often keep the brain perfused. It includes the anterior and posterior communicating arteries.

Watch out: many people have an incomplete circle, and berry aneurysms often form at its branch points.
cards.searchQuery: circle of Willis cerebral arterial circle collateral

cards.title: Which small bean-shaped lymphatic organs along lymph vessels filter lymph and house macrophages and lymphocytes?
cards.body:
Lymph nodes

Several afferent vessels bring lymph in, and one efferent vessel carries it out, so lymph slows as it passes through the node's sinuses. Nodes swell and become tender during infection as lymphocytes multiply.

Example: cancers often spread through lymphatics, so the nearest nodes (such as the axillary nodes for breast cancer) are examined.
cards.searchQuery: lymph nodes filter lymph macrophages lymphocytes

cards.title: Which is the largest lymphoid organ, lying in the left upper abdomen, that filters blood and removes old red blood cells?
cards.body:
Spleen

Its **red pulp** filters blood and destroys aged erythrocytes, while the **white pulp** contains lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne antigens.

Watch out: the spleen filters blood, not lymph. People without a spleen are at higher risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria.
cards.searchQuery: spleen red pulp white pulp filters blood

cards.title: Which lymphoid organ behind the sternum is where immature T lymphocytes mature?
cards.body:
Thymus

T cells learn to tolerate the body's own antigens here. The thymus is largest in children and shrinks after puberty.

Watch out: T cells are formed in red bone marrow but mature in the thymus, hence the T; B cells mature in the bone marrow.
cards.searchQuery: thymus T cell maturation lymphoid organ

cards.title: Which lymphatic vessel drains lymph from the whole body below the diaphragm and from the left side of the upper body into the left venous angle?
cards.body:
Thoracic duct

It starts at the **cisterna chyli** in the abdomen and empties into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. The shorter **right lymphatic duct** drains the right upper body.

Key idea: the thoracic duct is the body's largest lymphatic vessel.
cards.searchQuery: thoracic duct lymph drainage left venous angle

cards.title: Where in the respiratory tree does gas exchange first begin?
cards.body:
Respiratory bronchioles

The airway down to the terminal bronchioles is the **conducting zone**, which only transports air. Respiratory bronchioles have scattered alveoli, followed by alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs.

Watch out: the conducting zone's volume is the anatomical dead space, about 150 mL.
cards.searchQuery: respiratory bronchioles gas exchange begins respiratory zone

cards.title: What are the scroll-like bony ridges in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity that create turbulence to warm and humidify incoming air?
cards.body:
Nasal conchae (turbinates)

The superior, middle and inferior conchae increase surface area so air contacts the moist, vascular mucosa and trapped particles are caught by mucus.

Example: mucosa swelling around the conchae causes nasal congestion in a cold.
cards.searchQuery: nasal conchae turbinates warm humidify air

cards.title: Which is the largest cartilage of the larynx, forming the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple)?
cards.body:
Thyroid cartilage

It forms the anterior wall of the larynx and is usually more prominent in males. The **cricoid cartilage** below it is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.

Watch out: the epiglottis, made of elastic cartilage, covers the larynx during swallowing.
cards.searchQuery: thyroid cartilage larynx Adam's apple

cards.title: What shape are the hyaline cartilage rings that support the trachea, open toward the esophagus?
cards.body:
C-shaped

The open posterior part is closed by the **trachealis muscle**, a band of smooth muscle. The gap lets the esophagus bulge into the trachea when a food bolus passes.

Key idea: the rings keep the airway open, while the trachealis can narrow it, for example during coughing.
cards.searchQuery: trachea C-shaped cartilage rings trachealis muscle

cards.title: Which main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign objects usually lodge there?
cards.body:
Right main bronchus

Because it branches off the trachea at a smaller angle from vertical, aspirated objects tend to fall into the right bronchus and the right lower lobe.

Example: a swallowed peanut that enters the airway usually causes right-sided obstruction.
cards.searchQuery: right main bronchus aspiration wider shorter vertical

cards.title: How many lobes does the left lung have? Give the number only.
cards.body:
2

The left lung has a superior and an inferior lobe, with a **cardiac notch** to accommodate the heart. The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle and inferior).

Tip: the left lung has an extra part, the **lingula**, which is the equivalent of the right middle lobe.
cards.searchQuery: left lung lobes two cardiac notch lingula

cards.title: Which alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension in the alveoli?
cards.body:
Type II alveolar cells (septal cells)

Surfactant keeps the alveoli from collapsing at the end of expiration. It is not made until late in fetal development.

Example: premature infants may lack surfactant and develop respiratory distress syndrome.
Watch out: **type I cells** are thin squamous cells that make up most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange.
cards.searchQuery: type II alveolar cells surfactant septal cells

cards.title: What is the condition in which air enters the pleural space, causing the lung to collapse?
cards.body:
Pneumothorax

Normally the pleural pressure is slightly below atmospheric, which holds the lung against the chest wall. Air entering breaks this seal and the elastic lung recoils.

Example: a rib fracture that punctures the lung or a penetrating chest wound can cause pneumothorax.
cards.searchQuery: pneumothorax air in pleural space lung collapse

cards.title: Which lung volume is the air that remains in the lungs after a maximal exhalation and cannot be expelled?
cards.body:
Residual volume

It is about 1200 mL and keeps alveoli from collapsing completely. **Vital capacity** is the maximum air exhaled after a maximal inhalation and does not include it.

Watch out: vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve volume; total lung capacity includes residual volume as well.
cards.searchQuery: residual volume lung volumes after maximal exhalation

cards.title: From the lumen outward, what are the four main layers of the digestive tract wall?
cards.body:
Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa

The **mucosa** lines the lumen and absorbs and secretes. The **muscularis externa** has circular and longitudinal smooth muscle for motility, and the **serosa** is the outer connective tissue covering.

Watch out: the esophagus has an adventitia instead of a serosa, because most of it lies outside the peritoneal cavity.
cards.searchQuery: digestive tract wall four layers mucosa submucosa muscularis serosa

cards.title: Which nerve network, between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers of the gut wall, mainly controls gut motility?
cards.body:
Myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus)

It is part of the enteric nervous system and regulates peristalsis. The **submucosal plexus** (Meissner's plexus) mainly controls secretion and local blood flow.

Watch out: the enteric system can work without CNS input, though the parasympathetic vagus nerve modifies its activity.
cards.searchQuery: myenteric plexus Auerbach gut motility enteric nervous system

cards.title: Which glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the ileum?
cards.body:
Intrinsic factor

It binds vitamin $\mathrm{B_{12}}$ in the small intestine, and the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Without it, **pernicious anemia** develops.

Watch out: parietal cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor; chief cells secrete pepsinogen.
cards.searchQuery: intrinsic factor parietal cells vitamin B12 pernicious anemia

cards.title: Which hormone, secreted by G cells in the stomach antrum, stimulates parietal cells to secrete acid?
cards.body:
Gastrin

Gastrin release is triggered by stomach distension and peptides. It also stimulates gastric motility and growth of the gastric mucosa.

Why: acid secretion is self-limiting, because a very acidic antrum inhibits the G cells and stimulates somatostatin release.
cards.searchQuery: gastrin G cells stomach antrum acid secretion

cards.title: Which duodenal hormone, released in response to fats and proteins, causes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme release?
cards.body:
Cholecystokinin (CCK)

CCK is secreted by I cells in the duodenum. It also relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and slows gastric emptying, promoting satiety.

Mnemonic: **cholecysto** (gallbladder) + **kinin** (to move): it moves the gallbladder.
cards.searchQuery: cholecystokinin CCK gallbladder contraction pancreatic enzymes

cards.title: Which duodenal hormone, released in response to acidic chyme, stimulates the pancreas and bile ducts to secrete bicarbonate?
cards.body:
Secretin

Secretin is released by S cells in the duodenum. The bicarbonate neutralizes the acid chyme from the stomach, protecting the duodenum and providing the right pH for pancreatic enzymes.

Example: it was the first hormone ever discovered, in 1902.
cards.searchQuery: secretin duodenum bicarbonate pancreas acidic chyme

cards.title: Which segment of the small intestine absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts?
cards.body:
Ileum

The terminal ileum has specific transporters for the intrinsic factor-B12 complex and for bile salts, which are recycled through the enterohepatic circulation.

Example: after surgical removal of the terminal ileum (or in Crohn's disease affecting it), patients may develop B12 deficiency.
Watch out: most other nutrients are absorbed earlier, in the duodenum and jejunum.
cards.searchQuery: ileum absorbs vitamin B12 bile salts small intestine

cards.title: Which valve controls the passage of chyme from the small intestine into the large intestine?
cards.body:
Ileocecal valve

It lies where the ileum meets the cecum and prevents backflow of colon contents (with its bacteria) into the ileum.

Tip: the appendix attaches to the cecum, just below this valve.
cards.searchQuery: ileocecal valve ileum cecum junction

cards.title: What are the macrophages that line the liver sinusoids and remove bacteria and old cells from blood arriving from the gut?
cards.body:
Kupffer cells

Blood from the hepatic portal vein passes through the sinusoids, where Kupffer cells phagocytose bacteria and debris from the intestines.

Watch out: hepatocytes carry out metabolism and bile production; Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages.
cards.searchQuery: Kupffer cells liver macrophages sinusoids

cards.title: Deficiency of which brush-border enzyme causes lactose intolerance?
cards.body:
Lactase

Lactase on the intestinal microvilli cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose. Undigested lactose draws water into the gut and is fermented by bacteria, producing gas, bloating and diarrhea.

Watch out: this is an enzyme deficiency, not an immune reaction like a milk allergy.
cards.searchQuery: lactase deficiency lactose intolerance brush border

cards.title: What cup-shaped structure surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate?
cards.body:
Bowman's capsule

Together with the glomerulus it forms the **renal corpuscle**. The filtrate passes from the capsular space into the proximal convoluted tubule.

Watch out: the glomerulus is the capillary tuft; the capsule is the surrounding structure.
cards.searchQuery: Bowman's capsule glomerular capsule renal corpuscle

cards.title: Which cells of the glomerular capsule's inner layer have foot processes that form filtration slits around the glomerular capillaries?
cards.body:
Podocytes

The filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated capillary endothelium, the basement membrane and podocyte filtration slits. Large proteins and blood cells normally cannot pass.

Example: damage to this barrier (as in glomerulonephritis) leads to proteinuria or hematuria.
cards.searchQuery: podocytes filtration slits glomerulus foot processes

cards.title: Which enzyme do the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney release when blood pressure or renal perfusion falls?
cards.body:
Renin

Renin converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I. Angiotensin II, formed from it, then raises blood pressure and triggers aldosterone release.

Watch out: renin is an enzyme, not the active hormone; angiotensin II is the active product.
cards.searchQuery: renin juxtaglomerular cells renin-angiotensin system

cards.title: Which vessel carries blood away from the glomerulus?
cards.body:
Efferent arteriole

It is narrower than the afferent arteriole, which maintains the high glomerular pressure needed for filtration. Constricting it increases the glomerular filtration rate.

Mnemonic: **E**fferent = **E**xits; **A**fferent = **A**rrives.
cards.searchQuery: efferent arteriole glomerulus blood leaves

cards.title: Which part of the loop of Henle actively transports $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{K+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ out of the tubule but is impermeable to water?
cards.body:
Thick ascending limb

The $\ce{Na+}$-$\ce{K+}$-$2\ce{Cl-}$ cotransporter removes salt, diluting the tubular fluid and building the medullary concentration gradient. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block this transporter.

Watch out: the descending limb is permeable to water but not to solutes.
acceptedAnswers: ascending limb of loop of Henle
cards.searchQuery: thick ascending limb loop of Henle NKCC2 impermeable water

cards.title: Which enzyme, abundant on lung capillary endothelium, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II?
cards.body:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)

Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone release. ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril lower blood pressure by reducing angiotensin II.

Watch out: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors can cause a dry cough.
cards.searchQuery: angiotensin-converting enzyme ACE angiotensin I to II lung

cards.title: Which urethral sphincter is made of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary control?
cards.body:
External urethral sphincter

It is innervated by the somatic pudendal nerve. The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle and is involuntary.

Key idea: the micturition reflex is triggered by bladder stretch, but you can delay urination by contracting the external sphincter.
cards.searchQuery: external urethral sphincter voluntary skeletal muscle micturition

cards.title: What funnel-shaped space in the kidney collects urine from the major calyces and continues as the ureter?
cards.body:
Renal pelvis

Urine flows from the renal papillae into the minor calyces, major calyces, renal pelvis and then the ureter.

Example: a kidney stone can obstruct the ureter near the renal pelvis and cause severe flank pain.
cards.searchQuery: renal pelvis calyces ureter urine flow

cards.title: Which cells in the seminiferous tubules nourish developing sperm, form the blood-testis barrier and respond to FSH?
cards.body:
Sertoli cells

These "nurse cells" support spermatogenesis and secrete **inhibin**, which feeds back to the pituitary to reduce FSH. Tight junctions between them form the blood-testis barrier.

Watch out: Leydig cells lie between the tubules and make testosterone in response to LH.
cards.searchQuery: Sertoli cells seminiferous tubules blood-testis barrier FSH

cards.title: Which coiled tube on the posterior surface of the testis is where sperm mature and are stored?
cards.body:
Epididymis

Sperm leaving the testis are immotile. During transit through the epididymis (about 2 weeks) they gain motility and the ability to fertilize.

Key idea: sperm become fully functional only after ejaculation and exposure to female tract secretions (capacitation).
cards.searchQuery: epididymis sperm maturation storage

cards.title: In order, what is the path of sperm from production to exit from the male body?
cards.body:
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ductus (vas) deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra

Sperm form in the seminiferous tubules, pass through the rete testis to the epididymis, then travel up the ductus deferens, join seminal vesicle fluid in the ejaculatory duct, and exit via the urethra.

Mnemonic: **SEVEN UP**: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.
cards.searchQuery: path of sperm seminiferous tubules epididymis vas deferens urethra

cards.title: Which gland encircles the urethra just below the bladder, adds a milky, citrate-rich fluid to semen and can obstruct urine flow when enlarged?
cards.body:
Prostate

Prostatic fluid is milky and slightly acidic, makes up about a quarter to a third of semen volume and contains citrate, PSA and enzymes. Benign prostatic hyperplasia compresses the urethra, causing hesitancy and a weak stream.

Watch out: the seminal vesicles contribute most of the semen volume (about 60 percent), and their fluid is alkaline and fructose-rich.
cards.searchQuery: prostate gland urethra semen benign prostatic hyperplasia

cards.title: Which paired glands behind the bladder provide most of the semen volume, including fructose that nourishes sperm?
cards.body:
Seminal vesicles

Their secretion also contains prostaglandins and clotting proteins that help semen coagulate briefly after ejaculation. Each duct joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct.

Watch out: the bulbourethral glands add a small clear pre-ejaculate fluid to neutralize acidic urine remnants in the urethra.
cards.searchQuery: seminal vesicles fructose semen volume

cards.title: In which part of the uterine tube does fertilization usually occur?
cards.body:
Ampulla

The ampulla is the widest section, closer to the ovary than the uterus. The fertilized egg then travels to the uterus over several days and implants at about the blastocyst stage.

Watch out: if the embryo implants in the tube instead, it is an **ectopic pregnancy**, a medical emergency.
cards.searchQuery: fertilization site uterine tube ampulla

cards.title: Which layer of the uterine wall is the thick smooth muscle layer responsible for contractions during labor?
cards.body:
Myometrium

Oxytocin stimulates its contractions during labor. The innermost **endometrium** is the lining that is shed during menstruation, and the outer **perimetrium** is a serosal covering.

Example: uterine fibroids are benign tumors of the myometrium.
cards.searchQuery: myometrium uterine wall smooth muscle layer

cards.title: Which phase of the uterine (menstrual) cycle is dominated by progesterone, causing endometrial glands to secrete nutrients?
cards.body:
Secretory phase

This phase follows ovulation and matches the ovarian luteal phase, when the corpus luteum makes progesterone. If no implantation occurs, progesterone falls and menstruation begins.

Watch out: the **proliferative phase**, driven by estrogen, rebuilds the endometrium before ovulation.
cards.searchQuery: secretory phase uterine cycle progesterone endometrium

cards.title: Which follicle cells surround the oocyte, respond to FSH and convert androgens to estrogens with the enzyme aromatase?
cards.body:
Granulosa cells

The **theca cells** make androgens under LH stimulation, and the granulosa cells convert them to estradiol under FSH stimulation. This is the two-cell model of ovarian estrogen production.

Watch out: the granulosa cells also become the corpus luteum cells after ovulation, which make progesterone.
cards.searchQuery: granulosa cells aromatase estrogen ovarian follicle
